[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Ansible Privilege Escalation: Master become, become_user, and become_method"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, Ansible connects to your managed nodes and executes tasks using the permissions of the SSH user configured for the connection. However, many administrative tasks require elevated privileges, such as root access, to install packages, modify system configuration files, or manage services. Ansible handles this requirement seamlessly through privilege escalation."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding the Core Privilege Escalation Directives"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Privilege escalation in Ansible is controlled primarily by three directives: become, become_user, and become_method. Understanding how these directives interact allows you to securely manage user permissions at the play, block, or task level."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"become: A boolean value (true or false) that enables or disables privilege escalation for a task, block, or play."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"become_user: Specifies the target user you want to switch to. The default target user is root, but you can switch to any system user such as postgres or www-data."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"become_method: Defines the underlying system utility used to gain privileges. Common methods include sudo, su, doas, pbrun, and pfexec."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Practical Examples of Privilege Escalation"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can apply privilege escalation at various levels within your Ansible playbooks. The following example demonstrates enabling become globally for a task to install a software package as the root user."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"--- 
- name: Install Nginx Web Server
  hosts: webservers
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure nginx is at the latest version
      apt:
        name: nginx
        state: latest
      become: true"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"In many scenarios, you need to execute tasks as a non-root privileged user, such as managing a database or deploying application code. You can accomplish this by combining become with become_user."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"--- 
- name: Manage Database Configuration
  hosts: databases
  tasks:
    - name: Run a database migration script as the postgres user
      command: /usr/local/bin/migrate_db.sh
      become: true
      become_user: postgres"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Changing the Become Method"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"While sudo is the industry standard and default escalation method for most Linux distributions, you may encounter restricted environments that require alternative utilities like su or doas. You can override the default method using the become_method directive."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"--- 
- name: Execute task using su
  hosts: legacy_servers
  tasks:
    - name: Update system limits using su
      template:
        src: limits.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/security/limits.conf
      become: true
      become_method: su
      become_user: root"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Scope of Application"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Privilege escalation directives can be defined globally at the play level, scoped to a block of tasks, or applied granularly to a single task. Defining become at the play level eliminates repetition when every task in the playbook requires elevated privileges."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"--- 
- name: Playbook Level Escalation
  hosts: all
  become: true
  become_method: sudo
  tasks:
    - name: Create a system directory
      file:
        path: /opt/app
        state: directory
        mode: '0755'"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices and Troubleshooting"},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always ensure that the connecting SSH user has appropriate permissions configured in the /etc/sudoers file on the managed nodes without requiring an interactive password prompt."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"If sudo requires a password, pass it securely using the command line flag --ask-become-pass (-K) when executing your playbook."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid running entire plays with become: true unless strictly necessary, adhering to the principle of least privilege for better security posture."}]
